title: Learning by self-play
objectives: Train a value table by self-play and explain how AlphaZero extends the idea.

screens.title: Learning from your own games
screens.prose: One table $Q(n, k)$ plays both sides of Nim: the value of taking $k$ sticks from a pile of $n$, for the player who moves. After you take $k$ and leave $n'$, it is your opponent's turn, and your gain is their loss.
screens.question: Your opponent's best value at $n'$ is $0.8$. What target should update $Q(n, k)$?

hints.text: Zero-sum: what is good for them is bad for you.

feedback.correct: The target is $-0.8$: their best is your worst.
feedback.generic: Not quite. The game is zero-sum.

byKey.sign: You used their value as yours. Their win is your loss.
byKey.zero: The opponent's position is not neutral: it is worth 0.8 to them.

explain.text: The target is $-0.8$. Minimax with one table: $\text{target} = -\max_{k'} Q(n', k')$. It is l11's Q-learning target with the max replaced by the opponent's best, negated.

screens.title: Win rate against a stranger
screens.prose: The table learns by playing itself ($\alpha = 0.5$, $\varepsilon = 0.2$, random starting piles, seed 0). Every 10 episodes we froze it and played 200 games from 21 sticks, moving first, against a player who takes 1 to 3 at random. Slide to draw the curve.
screens.question: What happens to the win rate?

options.text: It climbs to 1: the table finds the winning rule
It stays near one half
options.why: Slide to the end: it reaches 1.

options.text: It falls as the table plays itself
options.why: Self-play here sharpens the table; the curve rises.

options.text: It is 1 from the start
options.why: At 0 episodes the table always takes 1 stick and wins only some games.

feedback.generic: Slide to the end and read the line.

explain.text: The untrained table wins 0.43 of games; once it has learned to leave multiples of 4, it wins every game. This run is seed 0.

screens.title: The last stick
screens.prose: If you take the last stick, the game ends and you have won. There is no opponent value to negate.
screens.question: What target updates $Q(n, k)$ when $k = n$?

byKey.neg: Taking the last stick wins in this game.
byKey.zero: The game is over and you won, so the value is 1, not 0.

explain.text: Terminal moves anchor the table: $Q(n, n) \to 1$ for $n \le 3$, and the negated targets carry that knowledge back to larger piles.

screens.title: What the table learns
screens.prose: After 500 episodes (seed 0), the greedy move from every pile that is not a multiple of 4 takes the remainder, $n \bmod 4$. At piles 4, 8, 12, 16 and 20 every move has a negative value.
screens.question: From a pile of 14, which take does the table choose?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Leave a multiple of 4.

byKey.one: That leaves 13, which wins for your opponent.

explain.text: The table recovers the multiples of 4 exactly: from 14 it takes 2. Where every move loses (a multiple of 4), every value is negative.

screens.title: Code self-play
screens.prose: Write the loop of `self_play_nim`: each episode starts from a random pile from 1 to 21 (`rng.randint`). Each move draws `rng.random()` and explores with chance $\varepsilon$ (`rng.choice`); otherwise it takes the greedy move, ties to the fewest sticks. Update $Q(n, k)$ towards 1 when it takes the last stick, else towards $-\max_{k'} Q(n', k')$.
screens.question: Complete `self_play_nim`.

widget.starter:
import random

def self_play_nim(episodes, alpha, eps, seed, top=21):
    """Q[(n, k)]: value of taking k from n for the player to move.
    Both sides use the same table."""
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    Q = {(n, k): 0.0 for n in range(1, top + 1) for k in (1, 2, 3) if k <= n}
    ...
    return Q

tests.call: all(max((k for k in (1, 2, 3) if k <= n), key=lambda k: Q[(n, k)]) == n % 4 for n in range(1, 22) if n % 4)
all((lambda Q: all(max((k for k in (1, 2, 3) if k <= n), key=lambda k: Q[(n, k)]) == n % 4 for n in range(1, 22) if n % 4))(self_play_nim(500, 0.5, 0.2, s)) for s in range(1, 5))

widget.how: Submit runs 5 hidden tests on 500 self-play episodes. For seeds 0 to 4, the greedy move from every pile that is not a multiple of 4 must take the remainder. Every move from a multiple of 4 must be valued below 0, and taking the last stick must be worth 1.

screens.title: It only beats itself
screens.prose: A team trains a trading agent by self-play and reports a 50% win rate against its own latest version as proof of progress.
screens.question: What is wrong with that test?

options.text: It should be tested against fixed opponents too
Nothing: 50% against itself is ideal
options.why: Two equal copies split their games whatever their skill: the number says nothing.

options.text: It needs more self-play games
options.why: More games against itself still cannot show skill.

options.text: It should lose more often
options.why: The win rate against itself is uninformative either way.

hints.text: What does a copy of yourself win against you?
Measure against opponents that do not change.

feedback.correct: Evaluate against fixed opponents: a random player, earlier versions, known strategies.
feedback.generic: Not quite. What can a win rate against itself show?

byKey.fine: You took 50% against itself as a result. Any agent scores that against its own copy.

explain.text: A self-play agent can also drift into habits that only work against itself. Fixed opponents, such as our random player, show real progress.

screens.title: AlphaGo and AlphaZero (reading)
screens.prose: Reading, not rebuilt: Silver et al. (2016) put two networks inside MCTS for Go. A **policy network** (this level's idea) gives prior chances for each move, steering selection; a **value network** (level 3's idea) scores positions instead of random playouts. AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol 4 games to 1 in 2016. AlphaZero (2018) learned Go, chess and shogi from self-play alone.

rows: Bonus weighted by the policy network

screens.question: In AlphaZero, what replaces the random playout of plain MCTS?

options.text: The value network's estimate of the position
The policy network's move chances
options.why: Those steer which children are tried; the value network replaces the playout.

options.text: Alpha-beta search to the end
options.why: Go is far too large for that.

options.text: A table of every position
options.why: Go has far too many positions for a table.

hints.text: Which step needs a guess at who will win?
The value network answers it directly.

feedback.correct: The value network replaces the playout.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Match each network to an MCTS step.

byKey.policy: You matched the wrong network. The policy network sets priors for selection.

explain.text: The policy network focuses selection; the value network replaces simulation. Self-play games then train both, so search and learning improve each other.

screens.title: Self-play
screens.prose: One table (or network) plays both sides: $$Q(n, k) \leftarrow Q(n, k) + \alpha\big[-\max_{k'} Q(n', k') - Q(n, k)\big],$$ with target 1 for taking the last stick. It needs no teacher and no expert games, only the rules and a fair way to test progress.
screens.question: Why does self-play need some exploration ($\varepsilon > 0$)?

options.text: To keep trying moves it has ruled out
To make each episode shorter
To beat a random player later
options.why: The greedy table beats it without exploring at test time.

options.text: It does not: greedy self-play is enough
options.why: Greedy play repeats the same lines and leaves other values untouched.

feedback.correct: Exploring keeps every value up to date, as in levels 1 and 3.

screens.title: A market of copies
screens.prose: A desk trains market-making agents by letting copies of one agent trade against each other. In simulation they earn steadily. Live, the market holds many different participants.
screens.question: What is the main risk?

options.text: They learned to exploit copies, not real flow
None: profits in self-play carry over
options.why: Self-play profits show how the agent does against itself, not against others.

options.text: Training was far too slow to finish
The market's rules differ
options.why: The rules can be the same; the opponents are what differ.

hints.text: Who were the counterparties in training?

feedback.correct: Test against fixed and replayed opponents before trusting self-play gains.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Who does the agent face live?

byKey.none: You trusted self-play profit. A market of identical agents can also move together and amplify each other.

explain.text: Self-play agents can co-adapt, and a market full of identical agents can crowd the same side. Replayed flow and scripted strategies are the fixed opponents a desk needs.

ideas: Self-play: one table plays both sides; the target after a move is minus the opponent's best value, or the result at the end.
On Nim, 500 self-play episodes (seeds 0 to 4) recover the rule exactly: take $n \bmod 4$, and every move from a multiple of 4 is valued below 0.
AlphaZero puts a policy network and a value network inside MCTS and trains both on self-play games (reading); test any self-play agent against fixed opponents.

formula.name: Self-play target
formula.tex: Q(n, k) \leftarrow Q(n, k) + \alpha\big[-\max_{k'} Q(n', k') - Q(n, k)\big]
formula.note: Target 1 when the move takes the last stick.

quiz.question: What do AlphaZero's networks replace in plain MCTS?

options.text: Uniform priors and random playouts
The search tree itself, entirely
The rules of the game it plays
The visit counts at the root
options.why: Visits are still counted and decide the move.

explain.text: The policy network weights the exploration bonus by learned move chances, and the value network scores leaf positions instead of random games.
